subject: burnt toast
title: What If You Always Ate Burnt Toast?

scenes.text: What if you always ate burnt toast? What makes it tasty is the problem.
Above about one hundred twenty degrees Celsius, sugars and an amino acid in bread react and form acrylamide.
The darker the toast, the more acrylamide. Swedish scientists first found it in food in 2002.
Experts list it as probably cancer-causing in humans, because high doses caused tumours in rats and mice.
But those doses were huge. Studies in people so far have found no consistent link.
So the UK's advice is simply to toast to golden, not black. That browning reaction is also why burnt toast tastes so good.

description:
What if you always ate burnt toast? Browning above about 120 degrees Celsius forms acrylamide, which IARC classes as probably carcinogenic to humans based on high-dose animal studies; human studies so far are inconclusive.
The UK Food Standards Agency's Go for Gold advice is to toast starchy foods to golden yellow or lighter.
